newsitem.title: GERMANY: DB Research - strong outlook for U.S. economy.
newsitem.headline: DB Research - strong outlook for U.S. economy.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve will raise key interest rates only moderately in the next twelve months, even if inflationary pressures increase, a report by Deutsche Bank Research said on Wednesday.

If inflation in the United States starts to accelerate, the Fed will lift rates by a maximum of 50 basis points, Peter Cornelius of DB Research, the research wing of Germany's biggest commercial bank, Deutsche Bank, said.

Cornelius said he did not think that the Fed would raise rates at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee on July 1 and 2, as economic data from the second quarter did not suggest such a course.

Moving into the seventh year of recovery, the U.S. economy was in excellent shape, DB Research said, and there were no signs of growth impetus tiring, but instead there were still signs of upwards momentum.

Real growth of four percent this year could be followed by growth of 3.4 percent in 1998. U.S. growth had a wide base and impetus was coming from private investments, private consumption and the construction industry.

The U.S. economy will outperform its production potential for the foreseeable future, DB Research said, but the big question was whether inflation could be kept at low levels given the high level of growth, low jobless numbers and rising capacity utilisation.
A number of commentators have said that because of the increase in global competition, the relationship between wages and inflation had systematically changed.
However, it did not make sense to assume that long-term there was no danger of higher inflation.

The research group said it was important to pay attention to unit wage costs in the U.S., which have only shown a mild increase so far, and see how they barely reflect the jobs market situation in the U.S.
The slow development of unit wage costs related to the fall in supplemental pay costs.
Real wages were showing the highest level of growth since the 1970s and were growing faster than inflation.
Growth in money supply was also a cause for concern, Cornelius said, as it had grown faster than gross domestic product in recent years.
